title: U.S. Army to detonate 68 barrels of unstable lead azide in Iowa on Wednesday after court clears plan
summary: The U.S. Army will detonate nearly five tons of degraded lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown on Wednesday morning, after the Eighth Circuit lifted its stay and President Trump briefly ordered a halt pending court and governor-elect approval.
content:
The United States Army will detonate nearly five tons of unstable explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday morning, after a federal appeals court cleared the way for the operation and President Donald Trump briefly intervened to halt it.

The controlled detonation of 68 barrels of lead azide — about 9,500 pounds of a volatile chemical used to set off military munitions — is scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time on Wednesday, November 25, at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, according to the Army and an emergency alert sent to phones in the area by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, [CNN reported](https://www.cnn.com/2026/11/24/us/iowa-lead-detonation-army).

The decision ends, for now, a five-day legal and political standoff over a stockpile that the Army says has become too dangerous to move, too dangerous to leave alone, and too dangerous to destroy any other way.

The lead azide has been stored at the Middletown plant for more than 20 years. Over that time, according to the Army and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), the material has recrystallized inside its containers, leaving it extremely unstable and sensitive to even slight friction or movement. Army officials have warned that it could detonate spontaneously — and that falling temperatures this week make that risk worse. In a court filing on Saturday, the government said there was an immediate risk the material would explode as temperatures in Iowa were expected to drop below 30 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 1 degree Celsius).

The Army notified the EPA of the degraded material in March, according to court filings, and received an emergency permit on November 13 authorizing a controlled detonation. The permit, issued under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act, runs through February 11, 2027. The plant itself, a World War II-era facility spanning roughly 19,000 acres in Des Moines County near the Illinois border, has produced artillery shells, warheads, mortars and other munitions for more than eight decades. Middletown, the town beside it, has a population of about 400.

The plan was announced to the public only on November 15, five days before the detonation was originally scheduled for Friday, November 20. The short notice drew immediate criticism from residents, health experts and elected officials in Iowa and neighboring Illinois. The Army warned that the blast could send a plume of toxic lead dust as far as 100 miles northeast of the plant, across farmland, homes and towns in both states.

Environmental groups moved quickly to stop it. On November 19, Earthjustice, acting for the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club's Iowa chapter, sued in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit, challenging the validity of the EPA's emergency permit. The groups argued that the permit was issued without adequate consideration of safer disposal alternatives or of the health risks to nearby communities, and that the Army had failed to show that blowing up the material in the open was the only option.

The court temporarily froze the permit on Thursday, forcing the Army to postpone the blast. On Monday, President Trump weighed in on Truth Social — days after [signalling he was inclined to resume major strikes on Iran](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/trump-inclined-resume-iran-strikes-after-new-year-november-2026) — saying he had ordered the military not to proceed until the Eighth Circuit agreed the operation could go forward and until Iowa's Democratic governor-elect, Rob Sand, agreed as well. "I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation," Trump wrote.

Trump added that if Sand or the courts did not agree, "we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation." Sand, who does not take office until January, responded on X that the administration "should make this decision based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago and have been on the ground in Middletown for weeks."

Hours after Trump's post, the Eighth Circuit lifted its stay. In an unsigned order, the judges concluded that the EPA had "adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead dust into the environment and mitigate the risks associated with potential exposure pathways," pointing to barriers erected around the storage area and to weather restrictions in the permit. The court also found that the Army had evaluated "a full range" of alternatives, including on-site chemical treatment, closed-chamber thermal treatment, relocating the individual drums, and detonating the material inside earth-covered magazines.

The judges acknowledged the danger of the planned blast, but weighed it against the danger of doing nothing. "We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide," they wrote. "However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place."

Late on Monday, Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said on X that the Army would proceed with the detonation on Wednesday morning as previously scheduled, based on forecast wind conditions. He said it was "the unanimous judgement" of the Army's personnel that the operation should go ahead, and the Army said in a statement that state, local and federal authorities were "unanimous" in their support.

The environmental groups have not said whether they will seek further legal action. Rachel Rintelmann, managing attorney for the groups, said in a statement on Monday night that the organizations were still reviewing the ruling. Their core objection remains the health risk: lead contamination can persist in soil and water for years, and children are especially vulnerable to lead exposure. The Army itself has said that "extensive modeling efforts predict that the potential level of lead particles in the air may be elevated" and that the detonation "will result in an air plume with some lead-containing particles which will disperse in the air and deposit on the ground."

The dispute has also revived a wider debate about how the American military disposes of old munitions. For decades, bases have relied on open burning and open detonation to destroy excess, unserviceable or obsolete explosives, as [Reuters explained](https://www.reuters.com/world/us/what-know-about-us-army-plans-blow-up-stockpile-lead-azide-iowa-2026-11-23/). The EPA and the National Academy of Sciences have identified safer alternatives, including enclosed treatment systems, but the practice remains common. Earthjustice argues that the Iowa case shows how that practice turns a storage failure into a public health problem: "The Army left 68 drums of a primary explosive to degrade for 20 years until it decided that the only safe option was to blow them up near populated areas," said Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau. "That turned the Army's storage management failure into a public health catastrophe for people in at least two states."

Iowa officials have been preparing for the blast for days. Governor Kim Reynolds' office announced on Friday that it had activated the State Emergency Operations Center to coordinate state agencies with the Army and the EPA. Senator-elect Josh Turek, who had called for a delay after hearing from residents worried about their health and safety, was among several Iowa officials who pressed for more time and more information.

For the residents of Middletown and the surrounding farm country — in a week when American industry also made headlines, with [Boeing winning a $7.4 billion order from China's Xiamen Airlines](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/boeing-xiamen-airlines-737-max-order-november-2026) — the immediate question is now practical: what happens on Wednesday morning, and what falls from the sky afterward. The Army says the detonation will take place inside earth-covered magazines, under layers of earth and concrete, and only under favorable wind conditions. Environmental groups and local officials say they will be watching the monitoring data — and the lead levels in the air, soil and water — long after the blast is over. The photo accompanying this article shows Middletown, Iowa, the small town beside the ammunition plant.

Further reporting on the operation and its aftermath is expected in the coming days, including any decision by the environmental groups on whether to appeal, and the results of the air and soil monitoring the EPA has required as a condition of the permit. For now, the Army's position is unchanged: the material cannot be moved, cannot be left where it is, and must be destroyed on Wednesday — before winter, and before it destroys itself.
